segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in the spirit of looking at irregularities in Spanish and how to deal with them and how to identify them, I wanted to spend a little bit of time speaking about making your own rules.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We've taught you a great amount of Spanish for you to be very conversational and reach fluency just through practice and listening in a very short amount of time if you get practicing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But we haven't looked at every single piece of content of Spanish, of course. But...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...the content that we've looked at has taken from every area of the language in an analytical way which will allow you to make your own rules when you come across things that you don't quite understand whilst you're practicing and exposing yourself to Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I just want to experiment a little bit in regards to that with you now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, I will present you with some imaginary situations where you see the language behaving in certain ways and I want you to make your own rule.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, it doesn't mean it's necessarily your own, somebody else might have come up with it before, but that you will figure out for yourself what is going on.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So for example, the word for "too" as in t-o-o is demasiado, demasiado.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Demasiado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's a bit of a long word, but if you break it up, it's easier to digest: you have de, más, "of more", y ado. And this is "too" (t-o-o), as in "too many".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Actually, de más can be used by itself. If you say «tengo cuatro de más», "I have four of more", «tengo cuatro de más», it means "I have four too many", "I have four spare", "I have four extra".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, demasiado means "too".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, imagine you hear these following sentences and I want you to work out what's happening here, why this word is behaving differently in different circumstances.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you might hear: «demasiadas casas».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might hear: «demasiados coches».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you might hear: «demasiado agresivo», «demasiado agresiva», and «demasiado agresivos».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Again. You might hear: «demasiadas casas», «demasiados coches».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Here, it's changing from the base form demasiado, no? «demasiadas casas», «demasiados coches».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then here, it's not: «demasiado agresivo», «demasiado agresiva», «demasiado agresivos».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So why in one situation is it changing and why in the other situation is it not?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: The only difference I see is that um it's related to nouns in the first two examples and in the second two, it's related to something descriptive...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Adjectives.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Adjectives.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Espectacular. Well done. Brilliant, that's it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We said that identifying what type of word we have will mostly be all we need to do to figure out what's going on. So we understand from this that when demasiado goes with a noun, it will change to match it:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: «demasiadas casas», «demasiados coches».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But when it goes with an adjective, it won't: «demasiado agresivo», «demasiado agresiva», «demasiado agresivos», «demasiado agresivas» is not changing.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we didn't learn that here, but we've been analytical enough of the language for you to figure that out by yourself.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, another example for you to figure out what's going on.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now the words: ala (wing), agua (water), and aula (hall or classroom) are all feminine words.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But we say: el ala (the wing), el agua (the water), and el aula (the classroom). What's going on?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it because the first letter of those words is a, and it would be weird to say um la ala?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You have other words that begin with a where you have la at the beginning, for example «la alfombra» (the carpet), «la almohada» (the pillow).

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you need to find something that's different between la almohada and la alfombra to el agua, el ala, el aula.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, the difference in this case is that it's just two just two syllables, perhaps?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That's it. They are two syllables and they begin and end in a.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, it's a very specific thing. It's not something that we're really going to spend time on learning here in this course, because it's very likely as well that you'll forget it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So what we have done throughout this course is given you the analytical skills to work it out by yourself and the confidence to make your own rules.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that's the rule: they're all feminine words, but they take el because they are two syllables and they begin and end with a.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we know that they are feminine because we say «el agua fría», the cold water, fría not frío. So we know they're actually feminine even though they're taking el. One more exercise like this.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "one" is uno, the word for "some" is alguno, and the word for "none" is ninguno. So we have uno, alguno, ninguno — one, some, none.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if I tell you: "how many do you want?", you will reply to me uno, or if you don't want any, ninguno.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if I say "one man", how do I say "one man" or "a man"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un hombre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un hombre. And if I say "some man", I say «algún hombre». And if I say "no man", I say «ningún hombre».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have uno, alguno, and ninguno: «no quiero ninguno», «quiero uno», «quiero alguno».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if I say "I want one car", for example: «quiero un coche», «quiero algún coche», «no quiero ningún coche».

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So what's happening there? Why does uno become un and why does alguno become algún?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Because a noun is following?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Because we have a noun following it, and it loses that last -o. So uno, alguno, ninguno become un, algún, ningún.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And you would notice that it doesn't happen with the feminine. So we have «una mujer» (a woman), «alguna mujer» (some woman), «ninguna mujer» (no woman).

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the point is just this: that we need to analyze the language that we are coming across, trying to pick out anything that we don't understand to tackle it so that we control it and we understand what's happening so that that element of the language doesn't control us.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very quickly, thinking in this way, you will get over your technical problems in the language. You will solve your technical problems.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then when you solve your technical problems in a specific language, then you can start to live freely in that language, and become somebody else in that language that is also you, but somebody else.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Because you are using this mechanism or this tool which, as we've said a few times, permits and obliges you to perceive and to express the world in a certain way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But before we can fully take advantage of that, we want to get over our technical difficulties, and this is achieved not through memorizing what is correct, but analyzing and understanding what is correct and finding why.
